title: Motion in One, Two, and Three Dimensions
short_intro: Motion is the continuous change in position of a body with respect to time and a given frame of reference. It is quantified using fundamental kinematic variables including displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Uniform and uniformly accelerated motion in a straight line, equations of motion, relative velocity, projectiles under gravity, and graphical analysis.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: General curvilinear motion in polar and Cartesian coordinates, vector treatment of kinematics, motion under central forces, and frames of reference including non-inertial systems.

prerequisites: Vector algebra (dot product, cross product, components)
Fundamental units and dimensions in SI

concept_notes.heading: Kinematic Quantities and Definitions
bullets: Displacement is a vector quantity representing the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position, with dimensions [L].
Average velocity is the ratio of total displacement to total time interval, whereas instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of the position vector r(t).
Acceleration measures the temporal rate of change of velocity vector, possessing components along the tangent and the normal to the trajectory.

concept_notes.heading: Motion with Uniform Acceleration
bullets: Under constant acceleration a, the kinematic equations are valid and independent of the mass of the moving body.
The area under the velocity-time graph represents the total displacement of the particle over the given time interval.
Free fall near the Earth's surface represents vertical motion under a constant downward gravitational acceleration g approx 9.8 m/s².

concept_notes.heading: Projectile Motion in Two Dimensions
bullets: Projectile motion under uniform gravity consists of independent horizontal motion with zero acceleration and vertical motion with constant downward acceleration g.
The trajectory of a projectile in a uniform gravitational field in the absence of air resistance is strictly parabolic.
The maximum horizontal range for a given initial launch speed is achieved at an angle of 45° to the horizontal.

concept_notes.heading: Relative Motion and Frames of Reference
bullets: Galilean transformation relates the position coordinates of a particle between two inertial frames moving with a constant relative velocity.
In non-inertial frames accelerating at a, fictitious forces such as the pseudo-force ma and the Coriolis force must be introduced to apply Newton's laws.
The relative velocity of body A with respect to body B is given vectorially by v<sub>AB</sub> = v<sub>A</sub> - v<sub>B</sub>.

derivations.title: Equation of Parabolic Trajectory for a Projectile
derivations.conditions: Uniform gravitational field, constant initial speed u, launch angle theta, zero air resistance
steps: Resolve initial velocity into components: u<sub>x</sub> = u cos(theta) and u<sub>y</sub> = u sin(theta).
Express horizontal position as a function of time t: x = (u cos(theta))t, yielding t = x / (u cos(theta)).
Substitute the expression for time t into the vertical position equation to eliminate time.

derivations.title: Derivation of Maximum Height and Time of Flight
derivations.conditions: Projectile launched from ground level with initial speed u at angle theta
steps: At maximum height H, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero: v<sub>y</sub> = u sin(theta) - gt<sub>up</sub> = 0.
Solve for time to reach maximum height: t<sub>up</sub> = (u sin(theta)) / g, and double it for total time of flight T = (2u sin(theta)) / g.
Substitute t<sub>up</sub> into the vertical displacement equation H = (u sin(theta))t<sub>up</sub> - (1/2)gt<sub>up</sub>².

graphs_and_experiments.title: Displacement-Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Position s on the vertical axis against time t on the horizontal axis for uniform, accelerated, and decelerated motion.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the tangent at any point on the curve yields the instantaneous velocity at that precise instant.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in TGT for identifying stationary bodies, constant velocity, and increasing acceleration phases.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Velocity-Time Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Velocity v on the vertical axis against time t on the horizontal axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the line gives the acceleration, and the net area enclosed between the curve and the time axis represents the total displacement.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via multi-stage numerical problems requiring total distance and displacement calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Projectile Trajectory Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Vertical height y versus horizontal distance x showing a symmetric parabolic arc.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the independence of horizontal and vertical motions under uniform gravity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate maximum height, time of flight, and coordinates at arbitrary points along the path.

solved_numericals.question: A stone is dropped from the top of a tower 125 m high. Calculate the time taken to reach the ground and its final velocity just before striking the ground. (Take g = 10 m/s²)
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: initial velocity u = 0, displacement s = 125 m, acceleration a = g = 10 m/s².
Use the kinematic equation s = ut + (1/2)gt²: 125 = 0 + (1/2)(10)t².
Solve for t: 5t² = 125 => t² = 25 => t = 5 s.
Calculate final velocity using v = u + gt: v = 0 + (10)(5) = 50 m/s.

solved_numericals.question: A projectile is fired with an initial velocity of 20 m/s at an angle of 30 degrees to the horizontal. Calculate the maximum height reached. (g = 10 m/s²)
solution_steps: Identify parameters: u = 20 m/s, theta = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
Recall the formula for maximum height: H = (u^2 sin^2(theta)) / (2g).

solved_numericals.question: The position vector of a particle is given by r(t) = (3t^2)i + (2t^3)j + 5k in SI units. Find the magnitude of its acceleration at t = 2 s.
solution_steps: Find velocity vector by differentiating position with respect to time: v(t) = dr/dt = (6t)i + (6t^2)j.
Find acceleration vector by differentiating velocity with respect to time: a(t) = dv/dt = (6)i + (12t)j.
Substitute t = 2 s into the acceleration vector: a(2) = 6i + (12 * 2)j = 6i + 24j.
Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration vector: |a| = sqrt(6^2 + 24^2) = sqrt(36 + 576) = sqrt(612) = 6 sqrt(17) m/s².

assumptions_and_limitations: Newtonian mechanics assumes classical spacetime where time is absolute and spatial measurements are independent of inertial reference frame speeds.
Air resistance is neglected in standard elementary projectile problems unless specified by a viscous drag force term.
The Earth is treated as an inertial frame for most elementary laboratory kinematics, ignoring Coriolis and centrifugal effects for short-duration local motions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, both velocity and acceleration are zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only the vertical component of velocity is zero; horizontal velocity remains constant, and vertical acceleration is always equal to g downward.
common_misconceptions.why: Gravity acts continuously throughout the entire flight trajectory, meaning acceleration never vanishes.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter objects in a vacuum.
common_misconceptions.correct: All objects fall with identical acceleration under gravity regardless of their mass.
common_misconceptions.why: Galileo's principle and Newton's second law show that gravitational force (mg) divided by mass (m) yields an acceleration independent of mass.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Distance and displacement are always equal in magnitude.
common_misconceptions.correct: Displacement is equal to distance only when motion occurs along a straight line in a single direction without turning back.
common_misconceptions.why: Distance is a scalar representing path length, whereas displacement is a vector connecting initial and final positions.

quick_revision: Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes, relying on position, velocity, and acceleration.
The slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration, and its area represents displacement.
Projectile motion combines uniform horizontal velocity with uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
Maximum projectile range on level ground occurs at a launch angle of 45 degrees.
